Italy Campaign. From nineteen forty-three to nineteen forty-five, the Allied invasion and liberation of Italy from Axis control extended from Sicily through the Italian peninsula to the borders of Germany. The campaign was one of World War Two's longest and costliest theaters, involving millions of troops, fighting through difficult terrain against entrenched German defenses, and demonstrating the challenges of amphibious invasion and mountain warfare while simultaneously destabilizing Italy's fascist regime.

Operation Husky in July nineteen forty-three saw American and British forces invade Sicily. Rapid conquest led to the fall of Benito Mussolini's fascist regime and a complex Italian surrender, complicated by German occupation of much of the peninsula. The invasion of mainland Italy began in September nineteen forty-three across the Strait of Messina. German forces under Field Marshal Albert Kesselring resisted fiercely, establishing defensive lines including the Gustav Line and Winter Line across the peninsula that halted Allied advance.

The Battle of Monte Cassino from January to May nineteen forty-four became a symbol of the campaign's brutality. Allied forces assaulted a fortified height for months at enormous cost, over one hundred thousand casualties, before finally capturing it. Polish troops ultimately took the ruins.

The Salerno landings in September nineteen forty-three nearly ended in disaster when German counterattacks almost drove the beachhead back into the sea. American reinforcements and naval gunfire support stabilized the landing and enabled breakout. Fighting extended up the peninsula for nearly two years. By mid-nineteen forty-four, the focus shifted northward toward the Gothic Line and eventually the Po Valley. German forces fought a delaying campaign, inflicting maximum casualties to buy time for defense of Germany proper.

The campaign tied down German forces that might otherwise have reinforced other theaters. Italy's surrender and shift to co-belligerent status complicated the political settlement of Southern Europe and left unresolved questions about Yugoslavia and Greece that would shape postwar European politics.
